name: Umbra Grey
lede: Umbra Grey is a dark olive grey recorded across three different color systems eighty years apart, and in our painting archive it is one of the most common hues.

sections.title: Three systems, one grey
sections.body:
Robert Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* places this hue on plate XLVI, at hue 13'''' and tone m, scanned from an aged, approximate plate [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files its nearest block as olive gray, and separately lists a near-duplicate, Fuscous-Black, only 1.8 units away [1]. RAL, founded in 1927, also lists a close match as RAL 7022 [1]. The books give no account of who first used the word "umbra" for this grey, so that origin is undocumented here [1].

Its nearest named neighbor in our library is a near-duplicate, Fuscous-Black, at a distance of only 1.8 units[1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this hue, as photographed, in 1,297 of 23,781 paintings (5.45 percent), more common than 88 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 102 of 1,674 paintings, at 1.8 times the expected rate for paintings from that century [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 42 percent of its 784 occurrences [2].

[[painter:arnoud-van-halen|Arnoud van Halen]] is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 12 of 50 of his works, 5.4 times his home museums' baseline [2]. The earliest matching painting is dated 1099, 813 years before Ridgway recorded the name in 1912, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[castor-grey]], [[grey-olive]] and [[traffic-grey-b]], at 3.1, 3.6 and 3.6 ΔE [2]. Among the standard greys, it is comparably dark to [[trooper]], though the two are not a close hue match [2].

origin.source: Ridgway, Color Standards and Color Nomenclature (1912)
